analysis.one_liner: Makes over-the-road bus drivers eligible for overtime pay and hour limits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was referred to, and no other senator signed on before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal wage law sets maximum work hours and requires overtime pay for most workers, but over-the-road bus drivers — drivers of the elevated-deck buses used for long-distance routes — have been exempt since 1938. This bill would remove that exemption, so bus companies would have to pay drivers time-and-a-half after long hours and cap how long they can work behind the wheel. It was introduced in July 2019 and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Over-the-road bus drivers gain the overtime pay and hour limits other covered workers already have, which means more pay for long trips and fewer forced marathon shifts. Passengers also gain a safety margin, because a driver who has hit a legal limit on hours cannot simply be worked longer.

how_it_helps.text: Over-the-road bus drivers are currently carved out of the Fair Labor Standards Act's maximum-hours rules, so they can be scheduled for very long workweeks with no overtime premium; the bill deletes that carve-out from the statute. [S2] [S3] [S1]
Removing the exemption means drivers of elevated-deck over-the-road buses would be covered by the same limits on hours that apply to other covered employees under the 1938 law. [S2] [S3] [S1]
Long hours behind the wheel are a documented fatigue risk in transportation; limiting them also reduces crash risk for bus passengers and everyone else on the road. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Over-the-road bus companies bear the cost: overtime premiums for long shifts and scheduling constraints that can require hiring more drivers. Some of that cost could pass through to ticket prices on thin-margin routes.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real costs on bus companies, which operate on thin margins on many routes; some operators could respond by raising fares, cutting schedules, or shifting drivers to classification schemes that avoid the new pay rules. [S3]

A federal overtime/hours mandate is a blunt tool: it applies uniformly to carriers of every size, without tailoring for short-haul versus long-haul operations, which critics of expanding motor-carrier coverage have argued can burden small operators. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward and well-targeted: a narrow class of workers gets the same wage-law protection nearly all other covered employees have, with a plausible safety payoff for passengers. The cost side is real but ordinary — overtime premiums and scheduling pressure on bus operators — and it does not obviously outweigh extending a protection other workers have had for decades. The bill is a one-line fix, not a carefully engineered regime, so it leaves questions like route economics unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee in July 2019, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Casey introduced the Driver Fatigue Prevention Act in the Senate on July 23, 2019. [S1] [S3]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. [S1] [S5]
No further action was recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion measure advancing. [S5] [S1]
No other senator cosponsored the bill during the Congress. [S4] [S1]
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died in committee. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Over-the-road bus operators are better off, because they avoided the overtime-pay and hours-limit costs the bill would have imposed. Bus drivers, whose exemption from federal hours protections continues, came out with nothing — and the bill's complete lack of cosponsors suggests driver fatigue was never a legislative priority in that Congress.

for.name: Sen. Bob Casey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Driver Fatigue Prevention Act to end the overtime exemption for over-the-road bus drivers.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the Fair Labor Standards Act
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 23, 2019 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before Congress ended.

against.name: The Senate as a whole
against.what_they_did: No senator signed on as a cosponsor and the chamber never took the bill up after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no recorded votes, so no party split ever took shape.

industries.note: The bill would end these companies' exemption from federal hours limits and overtime pay, raising labor costs and constraining long-shift scheduling. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against drivers' pay and passenger safety. [S3] [S2]

industries.industry: Long-distance bus passengers and road users
industries.note: Hours limits and overtime requirements are aimed at driver fatigue, a crash-risk factor; the public safety benefit comes alongside the drivers' wage gain. [S3]
